Today's big story: Could Anthropic Stock Fall 25%?

Most talk about Amazon.com this week is about its stake in Anthropic. This piece looks at something else. It asks what owning Amazon for ten years was really like.

The answer first. $1 million put into Amazon at the close on Friday, Nov 18, 2016 was worth $7,044,306 at Wednesday's close. That is a gain of 604.4%, or 21.6% a year. The same $1 million in QQQ grew to $6,024,248. QQQ is a fund that tracks the Nasdaq-100 index of large Nasdaq stocks.

The ride was much harder than the ending suggests. Amazon's worst fall took it down 56.1% between July 8, 2021 and Dec 28, 2022. It then needed 694 trading days from the peak to get back to its old high. QQQ, Alphabet and Microsoft each recovered faster from their own worst falls.

What did the 2022 fall do to the stake?

At Amazon's record close on July 8, 2021, the 2016 stake was worth $4,908,717. At the low on Dec 28, 2022, it was worth $2,152,705. The holder gave back $2,756,012 of paper gains. Even so, the stake was still worth more than twice the starting $1 million.

Watching $2,756,012 of gains disappear is hard to sit through. A smaller drop makes it easier to stay invested. Holding on is easier when your portfolio falls less than the market. For every dollar its benchmark lost, the Trefis High Quality (HQ) Portfolio lost about 81 cents on average. See the HQ record.

The wait was long as well. Amazon did not close above its July 2021 record close again until April 11, 2024. In calendar 2022 alone, the stock returned -49.6%. In calendar 2023 it returned 80.9%.

The stake's lowest dollar value came much earlier. Its lowest close in the ten years was $973,927 on Dec 2, 2016. It sat below the starting $1 million on only 9 trading days, all in the first weeks.

Why did Amazon fall so far in 2022?

Our data does not tie the fall to one cause, so we do not name one. The company's own figures show what the business went through in those years. Revenue still grew, from $469.8 billion in fiscal 2021 to $514.0 billion in fiscal 2022. Operating income, the profit from running the business, fell 50.8% from fiscal 2021 to fiscal 2022.

Fiscal 2022 also ended with a net loss of $2.7 billion. Net income is the profit left after every cost, tax and investment gain or loss. In fiscal 2023, operating income rose to $36.9 billion. By fiscal 2025 it had reached $80.0 billion.

How did Amazon's ride compare with Alphabet, Microsoft and QQQ?

Options trading begins Monday, letting traders hedge or short Anthropic, and the $83 IPO price becomes the key level to watch.

Cboe's JJ Kinahan went on CNBC before the bell Thursday with a bullish call: demand for Anthropic (NASDAQ:ANT) was running almost seven times the offering, and the first trade should land around $103 or $104, about 25% above the IPO price. Then he brought up the one deal anyone can compare this to: SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX).

jurvetson / Flickr

He missed the open. Anthropic priced at $83 and opened at $111.50 after a record $81.3B IPO raise. It touched $115.10, fell as low as $95.05, and by noon sat at $100.15, still up 20.66% from the offering price. Anyone who bought on the open is already under water.

SpaceX's Record Since Its Debut

Kinahan said SpaceX priced its IPO at $135, first traded at $150, and later traded at $105 two months after the debut. The full record looks worse for anyone who bought the opening. SpaceX hit $225.64 in the week ended June 18, bottomed at $104.83 on August 3, and closed Wednesday at $143.50. That is 10.84% below its $160.95 first-day close. Today it is off another 4.24%.

Released:The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income. It is a free guide from Fisher Investments covering what your retirement will really cost, where the cash flow should come from, and how much you can safely withdraw each year. Learn more here. Learn More Here › (sponsor)

Anthropic (NASDAQ:ANT) starts trading today. Yahoo Finance reports the AI developer priced its initial public offering at $83 per share. According to the company's own release, its Class A shares list on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol "ANT". Bloomberg reported that the offering tops SpaceX in size. For holders of the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ), which had $490.10 billion in net assets as of June 30, the key question is how quickly a listing this large could enter their fund. SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) went through the same process earlier this year, and its path gives QQQ holders a useful reference point.

nasakennedy / Flickr / Public Domain
How a Brand-New Stock Can Reach QQQ in Weeks

New listings normally need to wait. To qualify for the Nasdaq-100 Index, a stock must have traded for at least three full calendar months, not including its listing month. The index is then rebalanced once a year after the third Friday in December.

At Wednesday's close on Nov 18, Nvidia stood 36.9% below its October high. Alphabet was 29.8% below its May high. Meta Platforms was 20.7% below its September high.

Most coverage explains each fall on its own. This article looks at the full record instead. Since 2000, three or more of six big tech stocks fell 20% together in 12 separate episodes. SPY, the S&P 500 ETF, was higher 12 months later in 8 of the 11 that have a full year of data.

That sounds reassuring, but any day since 2000 gave about the same odds. SPY was higher a year later on 75.4% of all trading days. So falling giants have not, by themselves, been a signal either way. What split the good years from the bad was how long the leaders stayed down.

How Narrow Is Today's Fall?

Only three of the six are down 20% or more. Microsoft is 8.5% below its high. Amazon is 5.7% below, and Apple just 1.1%. SPY closed 6.3% below its Oct 6 high.

So the index has not followed the three stocks into a 20% fall. QQQ, the Nasdaq-100 ETF, sits in between, at 13.2% below its high.

The S&P 500 is only 6.3% off its high while three of its biggest names are down 20% or more. If you would rather your money leaned less on a few tech giants, steady income is another way to stay invested. Today's big story: Could Anthropic Stock Fall 25%?

$1 million put in VYM, the Vanguard High Dividend Yield ETF, at the Nov 18, 2016 close was worth $2,945,829 at Wednesday's close. That assumes every dividend was reinvested. It works out to 11.4% a year. An ETF, or exchange-traded fund, is a basket of stocks that trades like a single share.

Many investors see dividend funds as the safe, boring choice when tech stocks wobble. This piece looks at the ride, not just the end value. VYM had 4 falls of 10% or more in ten years. QQQ, the fund that tracks the Nasdaq-100 index, had 13. Yet in 2020, VYM fell further than QQQ and took longer to recover.

The cash was steady too. If you spent the dividends, you would now hold $2,175,790 in shares. You would also have collected $422,311 in cash along the way. The yearly cash rose from $33,020 in the first 12 months to $50,048 in the latest 12 months.

How bad was VYM's worst fall?

The worst fall came in 2020. From Jan 17 to Mar 23, 2020, VYM lost 35.2% with dividends reinvested. Counting from that peak, it needed 241 trading days to get back to its old high. QQQ lost 28.6% in its own 2020 fall. It was back at its high 73 trading days after its peak.

A fall that deep, followed by a wait that long, tests any holder's patience. Holding on is easier when your portfolio falls less than the market. For every dollar its benchmark lost, the Trefis High Quality (HQ) Portfolio lost about 81 cents on average. See the HQ record.

At the Mar 23, 2020 low, the $1 million in VYM was worth $926,763. Only two closes in ten years were below the starting $1 million. At QQQ's low that March, its $1 million was still worth $1,485,004. QQQ had simply built a bigger cushion first.

QQQ is the fund that holds the AI leaders. Say you put $1 million into it on Nov 18, 2021. You reinvested every dividend and never sold. At Wednesday's close, it was worth about $1.69 million.

That is the ending. The path to it was much harder.

How Far Did $1 Million In QQQ Fall?

It sat below $1 million for almost two years.

Six weeks after you bought, it started falling. By Nov 3, 2022, your million was worth $652,000. From January 2022, it stayed below what you paid for 487 trading days in a row. That is about 23 months. It did not get back above $1 million for good until Dec 12, 2023.

To get from $652,000 back to $1 million, QQQ needed a 53% gain. It got one, rising 54.9% in 2023. But nobody knew that in November 2022.

The swings have not stopped. On Oct 6, the same million was worth $1.95 million. Six weeks later, at the Nov 18 close, it was $1.69 million. That is $257,000 less. Across the whole five years, it was below $1 million on 41% of all trading days.

QQQ's million fell to $652,000 before it grew to $1.69 million. Growth is easier to hold on to when the rest of your money falls less. The Trefis Income Solution pays a dividend yield about 3x the S&P 500's, and it lost less than the S&P 500 in all 9 big selloffs since 2018. See the metrics.

What If A Fund Never Gets Back?

It happens.

ARKK is an innovation fund that rose 153% in 2020. It then turned $1 million into $263,000 by December 2022. It rose 69% in 2023, 8% in 2024 and 35% in 2025. That is three good years in a row. Yet at Wednesday's close, the million was still only $635,000. In five years, it never once closed back above $1 million. From $263,000, it needed to almost quadruple. From here, it still needs a 58% gain.

CALGARY, AB, Nov. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Canada News Group News Commentary - Wall Street heads into Thursday's session with the S&P 500 on its longest losing streak since June. The benchmark fell 16.90 points, or 0.23%, on Wednesday to 7,323.63, its fifth straight decline, according to CNBC, while the Nasdaq Composite rose 101.50 points, or 0.42%, to 24,429.88 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 561.25 points, or 1.11%, to 50,198.17. Week-to-date figures compare Wednesday's close with the close on Friday, November 13. Year-to-date figures compare it with the December 31, 2025 close. Both are calculated from Associated Press closing data.

S&P 500: 7,323.63. Week to date, down 238.04 points, or 3.15%. Year to date, up 478.13 points, or 6.98%.

Monday set the tone. The Nasdaq Composite fell 626.52 points, or 2.5%, to 24,509.76, and the S&P 500 fell 1.92% to 7,416.59 as technology stocks dropped sharply, according to the Associated Press and CNBC.

On Tuesday, the selling shifted toward the Dow, which fell 848.75 points, while the S&P 500 lost 76.06 points, by our arithmetic from AP closing data.

Wednesday split the indexes. Minutes from the Federal Reserve's October meeting, released in the afternoon, showed that almost all officials see further rate increases as likely appropriate, according to reports on the minutes, and Fed Governor Christopher Waller told CNBC the central bank may need a half-point increase in December. A drop of about 10% in one heavyweight health insurer accounted for about two-fifths of the Dow's decline, according to FXStreet, while the Nasdaq Composite and the Nasdaq-100 finished higher. The Fed's next policy decision is scheduled for December 9, according to its meeting calendar.

The pullback follows a stronger stretch. title: ANT Marks Momentous Occasion for Wall Street

ANT Marks Momentous Occasion for Wall Street
Mark Vickery

Thursday, November 19th, 2026

Pre-market futures are pleasingly in the green at this hour, ahead of an historic IPO that looks like the shot in the arm to market sentiment that investors have been waiting for. The Dow is +250 points at this hour, the Nasdaq is thrusting forward by +509 points, the S&P 500 is +77 and the small-cap Russell 2000 is +11 points presently.

It's a momentous day on Wall Street with the IPO on Anthropic — the first of the pure-play AI giants to go public. It will trade under the tick symbol "ANT" and will start at $83 per share. By initial haul, it's the biggest IPO of all time; we'll see over the course of the trading day how it compares with SpaceX's SPCX IPO back in June, which was previously the biggest.

The company priced ahead of its initial price range of $70-78 per share, which on the one hand shows terrific interest in this stock, but on the other looks to be putting the share price in a lofty clime to start. Its fully diluted valuation now registers $1.5 trillion (if 2026 has been an historic year in many ways, one of them is certainly that we no longer raise our eyebrows at TRILLION-DOLLAR IPOs). The company has roughly generated $80 billion from the sale of 980 million shares of the stock.

This ushers in a new realm for Wall Street, even if, like we saw with SpaceX over the summer, the heady price doesn't hold right away. So investors will be forgiven to not rush head-first into a massive buy of ANT stock today. But will it be worth owning? Based on its projection as being the most efficient enterprise agency ever devised, it would be pretty hard to reject this notion.

Weekly Jobless Claims Up from Multi-Year Lows

Initial Jobless Claims this Thursday morning (next week they'll come a day early, due to Thanksgiving) came in above 200K two straight weeks for only the first time since the week before Labor Day: +203K, up a tad from the upwardly revised +202K the previous week. These are still reflective of a robust labor market overall; we only have to look back to June to find new claims north of +220K.

Continuing Claims, reported a week in arrears, had a more pronounced jump week over week to +1.763 million from +1.699 million reported the prior week. Again, we don't put a lot of energy into worrying about this level; if anything, we appear to just be revering back to our "normal" lows on jobless claims.

Philly Fed Surprises to Downside

Meanwhile, the Philly Fed manufacturing survey for November this morning came in at about a third of projections: +6.3, compared to estimates of +18. It's the third-straight month lower, off August's robust +47.4. We recall a similar move in the November print on Empire State manufacturing early this week. Are we really slowing down in East Coast manufacturing business so soon?
